title: Astronomy: Solar System and Stars
description: For beginning astronomy learners: planets, moons, small bodies, seasons, eclipses, the Sun, and stellar life cycles. Focuses on durable concepts rather than changing discovery counts.

sources.name: NASA Science: Solar System
sources.license: NASA public educational reference; original wording

cards.front: What is the Solar System?
cards.back: The Sun and the bodies gravitationally associated with it, including planets, dwarf planets, moons, and small bodies.

cards.front: What object contains most of the Solar System's mass?
cards.back: The Sun, with roughly 99.8 percent of the total mass.

cards.front: List the eight planets outward from the Sun.
cards.back: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

cards.front: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
cards.back: Mercury.

cards.front: Which planet is largest by diameter?
cards.back: Jupiter.

cards.front: Which planet is smallest among the eight planets?
cards.back: Mercury.

cards.front: Which planet has the highest average surface temperature?
cards.back: Venus, because of its dense greenhouse atmosphere.

cards.front: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
cards.back: Mars, whose reddish surface contains iron oxides.

cards.front: Which planet has the most visually prominent ring system?
cards.back: Saturn. All four giant planets have rings.

cards.front: Which planet rotates with an axial tilt close to 98 degrees?
cards.back: Uranus, which effectively rotates on its side.

cards.front: Which planet is farthest from the Sun among the eight planets?
cards.back: Neptune.

cards.front: What are the four terrestrial planets?
cards.back: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars; they have predominantly rocky bodies and solid surfaces.

cards.front: Which two planets are called gas giants?
cards.back: Jupiter and Saturn, whose bulk compositions are dominated by hydrogen and helium.

cards.front: Which two planets are called ice giants?
cards.back: Uranus and Neptune; their interiors contain a greater proportion of heavier volatile materials than Jupiter and Saturn.

cards.front: What is an astronomical unit?
cards.back: A length defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 meters, approximately the Earth-Sun distance.

cards.front: What is a light-year?
cards.back: The distance light travels in vacuum in one Julian year, about 9.46 trillion kilometers.
cards.hint: Despite its name, it measures a length.

cards.front: Is a light-year a unit of time?
cards.back: No. It is a unit of distance.

cards.front: What is an orbit?
cards.back: A path followed by one body under the gravitational influence of another body or system.

cards.front: What is rotation?
cards.back: Spinning about an axis.

cards.front: What is revolution in astronomy?
cards.back: Motion around another body, such as a planet orbiting the Sun.

cards.front: What mainly causes Earth's seasons?
cards.back: Earth's axial tilt changes the Sun's angle and the length of daylight over the year.
cards.hint: Think about the orientation of Earth's axis.

cards.front: Why are Northern and Southern Hemisphere seasons opposite?
cards.back: When one hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, the other tilts away.

cards.front: What is an equinox?
cards.back: One of the two times each year when the Sun crosses the celestial equator; day and night lengths are approximately similar.

cards.front: What is a solstice?
cards.back: One of the two times each year when the Sun reaches its greatest northward or southward declination, marking extremes of seasonal daylight.

cards.front: What is perihelion?
cards.back: The point in an orbit around the Sun nearest the Sun.

cards.front: What is aphelion?
cards.back: The point in an orbit around the Sun farthest from the Sun.

cards.front: What does orbital eccentricity describe?
cards.back: How much an orbit departs from a circle; a circular orbit has eccentricity zero.

cards.front: What does Kepler's first law say about a planet's orbit?
cards.back: It is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus in the ideal two-body approximation.

cards.front: What does Kepler's second law imply about orbital speed?
cards.back: A planet moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion, sweeping equal areas in equal times.

cards.front: What does Kepler's third law compare?
cards.back: For objects orbiting the same dominant mass, orbital period squared is proportional to semimajor axis cubed.

cards.front: Why does Mercury have extreme day-night surface temperature differences?
cards.back: It has almost no atmosphere to redistribute heat and a very slow solar day.

cards.front: Does Mercury have any natural moons?
cards.back: No.

cards.front: Does Venus have any natural moons?
cards.back: No.

cards.front: What is unusual about Venus's rotation direction?
cards.back: Venus rotates retrograde relative to most planets, with the Sun appearing to rise in the west at its surface.

cards.front: What gas dominates Venus's atmosphere?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide.

cards.front: What is the greenhouse effect?
cards.back: Atmospheric absorption and re-emission of outgoing infrared radiation that raises surface and lower-atmosphere temperatures.

cards.front: What is distinctive about Earth's surface water?
cards.back: Earth has extensive stable liquid-water oceans at its surface.

cards.front: What gas is most abundant in Earth's dry atmosphere?
cards.back: Nitrogen, making up about 78 percent by volume.

cards.front: What gas is second most abundant in Earth's dry atmosphere?
cards.back: Oxygen, making up about 21 percent by volume.

cards.front: What is Earth's natural satellite called?
cards.back: The Moon.

cards.front: What causes the phases of the Moon?
cards.back: The changing fraction of its sunlit half visible from Earth as it orbits.

cards.front: Does Earth's shadow cause the ordinary lunar phases?
cards.back: No. Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse, not the usual monthly phases.

cards.front: What is a new moon?
cards.back: The phase when the Moon is near the Sun's direction in the sky and its illuminated side mostly faces away from Earth.

cards.front: What is a full moon?
cards.back: The phase when the Moon is opposite the Sun in the sky and its Earth-facing side is almost fully illuminated.

cards.front: What does waxing mean for the Moon?
cards.back: The visible illuminated portion is increasing.

cards.front: What does waning mean for the Moon?
cards.back: The visible illuminated portion is decreasing.

cards.front: Why do we see nearly the same side of the Moon?
cards.back: It rotates once per orbit relative to distant stars, a state called synchronous rotation.

cards.front: Is the Moon's far side permanently dark?
cards.back: No. Both near and far sides experience sunlight and darkness over a lunar day.

cards.front: What is a solar eclipse?
cards.back: An alignment in which the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks some or all of the Sun for observers in part of its shadow.

cards.front: What is a lunar eclipse?
cards.back: An alignment in which the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.

cards.front: Why do eclipses not occur at every new and full moon?
cards.back: The Moon's orbital plane is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane, so the bodies usually do not line up precisely.

cards.front: What are lunar maria?
cards.back: Dark basaltic plains formed by ancient lava flows; the name means seas, but they are not water oceans.

cards.front: What mainly causes Earth's ocean tides?
cards.back: Differences in gravitational pull across Earth, mainly from the Moon and also from the Sun.

cards.front: What are spring tides?
cards.back: Tides with a larger range around new and full moon, when solar and lunar tidal effects reinforce each other.

cards.front: What are neap tides?
cards.back: Tides with a smaller range around first and third quarter, when solar and lunar tidal effects partly oppose each other.

cards.front: What gas dominates the thin Martian atmosphere?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide.

cards.front: What are Mars's two moons?
cards.back: Phobos and Deimos.

cards.front: What is Olympus Mons?
cards.back: An enormous shield volcano on Mars.

cards.front: What is Valles Marineris?
cards.back: A vast canyon system on Mars.

cards.front: What evidence indicates that liquid water once flowed on Mars?
cards.back: Ancient channels, deltas, lake deposits, and water-altered minerals support past liquid water.

cards.front: What lies mainly between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter?
cards.back: The main asteroid belt.

cards.front: What is Ceres?
cards.back: A dwarf planet and the largest object in the main asteroid belt.

cards.front: What is an asteroid?
cards.back: A relatively small, mostly rocky or metallic body orbiting the Sun; many occupy the main belt.

cards.front: What is a comet?
cards.back: A small body rich in volatile ices that can develop a coma and tails when heated near the Sun.

cards.front: Why do comet tails generally point away from the Sun?
cards.back: Solar radiation pressure and the solar wind push material away; dust tails may curve along the orbit.

cards.front: What is a comet's nucleus?
cards.back: Its solid central body of ice, dust, and rocky material.

cards.front: What is a comet's coma?
cards.back: The diffuse envelope of gas and dust around its active nucleus.

cards.front: What is a meteoroid?
cards.back: A small natural solid body traveling through space, smaller than typical asteroids.

cards.front: What is a meteor?
cards.back: The luminous atmospheric phenomenon produced when a meteoroid enters at high speed.

cards.front: What is a meteorite?
cards.back: Material from a meteoroid that survives passage through an atmosphere and reaches the ground.

cards.front: What produces many annual meteor showers?
cards.back: Earth passing through streams of debris, commonly left along comet orbits.

cards.front: What is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
cards.back: A long-lived giant atmospheric storm.

cards.front: What are Jupiter's four Galilean moons?
cards.back: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

cards.front: Which moon is the largest in the Solar System?
cards.back: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter.

cards.front: Which Galilean moon is especially volcanically active?
cards.back: Io, heated strongly by tidal effects.

cards.front: Which Galilean moon has an icy surface over a likely global ocean?
cards.back: Europa.

cards.front: What are Saturn's main rings mostly made of?
cards.back: Countless particles composed largely of water ice, ranging from tiny grains to much larger pieces.

cards.front: Which Saturn moon has a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere?
cards.back: Titan.

cards.front: What liquids fill lakes and seas on Titan's surface?
cards.back: Mainly methane and ethane, rather than liquid water.

cards.front: Which Saturn moon sends water-rich plumes into space?
cards.back: Enceladus, through fractures near its south pole.

cards.front: What helps give Uranus and Neptune their blue-green colors?
cards.back: Methane absorbs red light in their atmospheres; aerosols and atmospheric structure also affect the observed colors.

cards.front: What is Neptune's largest moon?
cards.back: Triton.

cards.front: What is unusual about Triton's orbit?
cards.back: It is retrograde, moving opposite Neptune's rotation, supporting a captured origin.

cards.front: What is the Kuiper Belt?
cards.back: A region beyond Neptune containing many icy bodies, including Pluto.

cards.front: What is Pluto classified as?
cards.back: A dwarf planet.

cards.front: Why is Pluto not one of the eight planets under the IAU definition?
cards.back: It has not gravitationally cleared its orbital neighborhood, although it orbits the Sun and is nearly round.

cards.front: What is Charon?
cards.back: Pluto's largest moon.

cards.front: What is the Oort Cloud?
cards.back: A proposed distant, roughly spherical reservoir of icy bodies that can supply long-period comets.

cards.front: What is the heliosphere?
cards.back: The region of space dominated by the solar wind and the Sun's magnetic influence.

cards.front: What is the solar wind?
cards.back: A stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun's outer atmosphere.

cards.front: What is the Sun's energy source?
cards.back: Nuclear fusion in its core, primarily converting hydrogen into helium.

cards.front: What is the Sun mainly made of?
cards.back: Hydrogen and helium.

cards.front: What is the photosphere?
cards.back: The layer of the Sun from which most visible light escapes, often called its visible surface.

cards.front: What is the solar corona?
cards.back: The Sun's hot, tenuous outer atmosphere.

cards.front: What are sunspots?
cards.back: Relatively cool, dark-looking photospheric regions associated with strong magnetic fields.

cards.front: What is a solar flare?
cards.back: A sudden release of magnetic energy in the Sun's atmosphere that produces intense radiation.

cards.front: What is a coronal mass ejection?
cards.back: A large expulsion of magnetized plasma from the Sun's corona.

cards.front: What causes auroras on Earth?
cards.back: Charged particles excite atmospheric gases, usually after being guided into polar regions by Earth's magnetic environment.

cards.front: What is a star?
cards.back: A luminous self-gravitating ball of plasma; ordinary main-sequence stars generate core energy through hydrogen fusion.

cards.front: What is a nebula?
cards.back: An interstellar cloud of gas and dust, which may be involved in star formation or stellar remains.

cards.front: What is a protostar?
cards.back: A contracting young stellar object that has not yet reached stable main-sequence hydrogen fusion.

cards.front: What is the main sequence?
cards.back: The phase and diagram band occupied by stars stably fusing hydrogen in their cores.

cards.front: What stellar property most strongly sets a star's main-sequence lifetime?
cards.back: Its mass. Higher-mass stars consume fuel much faster and have shorter main-sequence lifetimes.

cards.front: Which visible star color generally indicates a hotter surface: blue or red?
cards.back: Blue. Red stars generally have cooler photospheres.

cards.front: What is stellar luminosity?
cards.back: A star's total emitted power, independent of an observer's distance.

cards.front: What is apparent brightness?
cards.back: The amount of a source's light received per unit area by an observer; it depends on luminosity and distance.

cards.front: What happens to received brightness if distance doubles, ignoring absorption?
cards.back: It falls to one quarter, by the inverse-square law.

cards.front: What is a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram?
cards.back: A plot comparing stellar luminosity with surface temperature or a related spectral measure.

cards.front: What is a red giant?
cards.back: An evolved star with an expanded, relatively cool outer envelope and high luminosity.

cards.front: What is a white dwarf?
cards.back: A dense stellar remnant supported mainly by electron degeneracy pressure, with no sustained core fusion.

cards.front: What is a planetary nebula?
cards.back: An expanding, glowing envelope expelled by an evolved low- or intermediate-mass star; it is unrelated to planet formation.

cards.front: What is a supernova?
cards.back: A powerful stellar explosion, caused by mechanisms such as core collapse or thermonuclear disruption.

cards.front: What is a neutron star?
cards.back: An extremely dense stellar remnant supported by dense nuclear matter, often formed in a core-collapse supernova.

cards.front: What is a pulsar?
cards.back: A rotating neutron star whose beamed emission sweeps across Earth as regularly observed pulses.

cards.front: What is a black hole?
cards.back: A region of spacetime with an event horizon beyond which outward light signals cannot reach distant observers.

cards.front: What is a black hole's event horizon?
cards.back: The boundary separating events that can send signals to distant observers from those that cannot.

cards.front: What is a binary star system?
cards.back: Two stars gravitationally bound and orbiting their common center of mass.

cards.front: What is an exoplanet?
cards.back: A planet orbiting a star outside the Solar System, in the usual observational use of the term.

cards.front: What is the transit method of exoplanet detection?
cards.back: Detecting periodic dips in a star's brightness when an orbiting planet crosses its visible disk.

cards.front: What is the radial-velocity method of exoplanet detection?
cards.back: Detecting periodic shifts in stellar spectral lines caused by a star's motion toward and away from us under a companion's gravitational influence.
